etymology: From “liturgy” (Greek leitourgia, public service); the Divine Liturgy attributed to John Chrysostom, the principal eucharistic service of the Eastern Orthodox church.
biblical_def: The Liturgy of Chrysostom is the Divine Liturgy attributed to John Chrysostom, the principal and most frequently used eucharistic service of the Eastern Orthodox church, fixed in form by the early centuries and used to this day. It is a service of great antiquity, reverence, and beauty, rich in Scripture, prayer, and the praise of the Holy Trinity, ordering the worship of the Eastern church through the year. The dictionary treats it as a matter of the principles of worship. Much in the liturgy reflects a true reverence: it is saturated with the words of Scripture and the Psalms, it confesses the Trinity and the incarnation in glorious terms, and it observes the apostolic rule that all things be done decently and in order. The offering of the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of the lips giving thanks to His name, is the heart of Christian worship in every age. Yet the dictionary, holding the regulative principle and the Reformed doctrine of the Lord's Supper, marks its grave departures. The liturgy treats the Supper as a propitiatory sacrifice offered by a priest, against the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ; it invokes the prayers of Mary and the saints; it is bound up with the veneration of icons; and it teaches a eucharistic doctrine the Reformed reject. The dictionary applies its rule for the Eastern church: respect what is preserved—Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy, the word-saturated reverence—and name what departs—the sacrificing priesthood, the invocation of saints, and a worship that, however beautiful, mingles the commandments of men with the worship of God. Worship must be in spirit and in truth; the dictionary honours the truth the liturgy preserves and names the additions it must reject.
webster_summary: The Divine Liturgy attributed to John Chrysostom, chief eucharistic service of Eastern Orthodoxy; honoured for its Scripture-rich, Trinitarian reverence, yet rejected where it makes the Supper a sacrifice, invokes saints, and venerates icons.

corruption_summary: The liturgy preserves Trinitarian reverence yet makes the Supper a propitiatory sacrifice, invokes Mary and the saints, and is bound to icon-veneration—mingling the commandments of men with the worship of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary honours what the Liturgy of Chrysostom preserves. It is an ancient and reverent service, saturated with Scripture and the Psalms, confessing the Holy Trinity and the incarnation in glorious terms, and observing the apostolic rule that worship be done decently and in order. In an age of casual and self-centred worship, its gravity, its word-centredness, and its God-ward focus are worth honouring, and the Eastern church has through it preserved much true praise of the triune God.

Yet the dictionary names its grave departures from Scripture without manufacturing grievance. The liturgy treats the Lord's Supper as a propitiatory sacrifice offered anew by a priest, against the once-for-all and all-sufficient sacrifice of Christ; it addresses prayers to Mary and the saints, trespassing on the one Mediator; and it is woven together with the veneration of icons, which the dictionary rejects per the second commandment. The Lord warned that worship which teaches for doctrines the commandments of men is vain. The dictionary applies its rule for the Eastern church—respect the Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy preserved, name the sacrificing priesthood, the invocation of saints, and the icon-veneration as the corruptions to be reformed by the Word of God.

etymology: From Rome; both the New Testament church of believers at Rome and the later Church of Rome that developed into the Roman Catholic communion.
biblical_def: “The Roman church” names two distinct things the dictionary is careful not to confuse: the New Testament congregation of believers at Rome to whom Paul wrote his greatest epistle, and the later Church of Rome that developed, through the medieval centuries, into the Roman Catholic communion. The apostolic church at Rome was a true church of Jesus Christ, beloved of God, called to be saints, whose faith was spoken of throughout the whole world, and to whom Paul unfolded the gospel of justification by faith. That church the dictionary honours without reserve. The later Church of Rome is another matter. Though it preserved many genuine Christian doctrines—the Trinity, the incarnation, the Chalcedonian Christology—it accumulated over centuries the corruptions the Reformation called the church away from: the papal monarchy, the treasury of merit, indulgences, purgatory, transubstantiation, the Marian dogmas, and above all the denial of justification by faith alone, anathematized at Trent. The dictionary holds the historic Protestant judgment, balancing two truths. Rome is not nothing: it retains the Scriptures, the catholic creeds, and the name of Christ, and there have been and are within it souls savingly trusting Christ despite its system. Yet Rome as a system has so corrupted the gospel that the Reformers were right to separate, and the apostle's warning stands: though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel, let him be accursed. The dictionary marks them which cause divisions contrary to the doctrine of the apostles, and calls the church to hold fast the gospel of free grace the Roman church at Rome first received, and the Church of Rome later obscured.
webster_summary: Both the New Testament church of believers at Rome (honoured without reserve) and the later Church of Rome that became the Roman Catholic communion; the latter retains the creeds yet so corrupted the gospel of free grace that the Reformers rightly separated.

corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary distinguishes carefully and judges justly. The New Testament church at Rome was a true church, beloved of God, whose faith was renowned and to whom Paul wrote the gospel of grace; it is honoured without reserve. And the later Church of Rome is not nothing: it preserved the Scriptures, the catholic creeds, the doctrines of the Trinity and the incarnation, and the name of Christ, and there have been within it souls savingly trusting the Saviour despite its system. The dictionary does not deny the genuine Christian truth Rome retained.

Yet the dictionary holds, with the Reformers, that the Church of Rome as a system so corrupted the gospel that separation was both right and necessary. The papal monarchy usurped the headship of Christ; the treasury of merit, indulgences, and purgatory denied the sufficiency of the cross; transubstantiation and the Mass corrupted the Supper; the Marian dogmas robbed Christ of glory; and Trent anathematized the very heart of the gospel, justification by faith alone. The apostle's warning is decisive: though an angel from heaven preach any other gospel, let him be accursed. The dictionary calls the church to mark and avoid the divisions Rome introduced contrary to apostolic doctrine, and to hold fast the gospel of free grace the church at Rome first received.

pos: proper noun (a city of the Reformation)
etymology: The Swiss city (German Zürich) where Huldrych Zwingli led the first Reformed Reformation from 1519, making it a fountainhead of the Reformed tradition.
biblical_def: Zurich was the Swiss city where Huldrych Zwingli, appointed people's priest at the Great Minster in 1519, led the first Reformed Reformation, making it a fountainhead of the Reformed (as distinct from the Lutheran) tradition. Zwingli began not with a theological crisis like Luther's but with the preaching of Scripture: he set aside the prescribed lectionary and preached straight through the books of the Bible, beginning with Matthew, and from that exposition of the Word the reform of Zurich flowed. Under his leadership and the city council's, the Mass was abolished, images and relics were removed from the churches, monasticism was ended, and worship was reordered to the simplicity the Reformed read in Scripture. The dictionary honours Zurich as a witness to the formal principle of the Reformation: that Scripture alone is the rule of faith and worship, that the word of God is truth and a lamp unto the feet, and that the church is to prove all things and hold fast that which is good. The reform of Zurich embodied the conviction that what Scripture does not warrant in worship is not to be imposed—the seed of the regulative principle the Reformed tradition would develop. The dictionary notes, without idealizing, the tragedies of Zurich's reform: Zwingli's death in battle at Kappel in 1531, the failure to agree with Luther on the Supper at the Marburg Colloquy, and the harsh persecution of the Anabaptists who arose there seeking a believers' church and believers' baptism—a persecution the Baptist tradition remembers with sorrow. Yet Zurich stands as the cradle of the Reformed faith, where the recovered Word of God reformed a city.
webster_summary: The Swiss city where Zwingli led the first Reformed Reformation from 1519 by preaching straight through Scripture; a fountainhead of the Reformed tradition and the regulative principle, though marked by the Marburg failure and the persecution of the Anabaptists.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the formal principle of the Reformation: Scripture alone as the rule of faith and worship. Zurich's reform began with the simple, revolutionary act of preaching straight through the books of the Bible, and from that exposition of the Word flowed the abolition of the Mass, the removal of images, and the reordering of worship. The dictionary honours Zurich as the cradle of the Reformed tradition and a witness that the recovered Word of God is the engine of all true reformation: thy word is truth, and a lamp unto the feet.

Yet the dictionary does not idealize the reform. Zwingli and the Lutherans failed to agree on the Lord's Supper at the Marburg Colloquy, fracturing the Protestant cause; Zwingli himself died sword in hand at the battle of Kappel, a tangling of the gospel with the sword the dictionary notes with sorrow. Most painfully for the Baptist tradition, it was at Zurich that the first Anabaptists arose, seeking a church of believers and believers' baptism, and were harshly persecuted, some drowned. The dictionary honours the Reformed recovery of the Word at Zurich while mourning the persecution of those who, following the same Word, sought a regenerate church—a lesson that even a true reformation must be reformed further by Scripture.

pos: proper noun (a city of the Reformation)
etymology: The city on the Rhine (German Straßburg), a chief centre of the early Reformation under Martin Bucer, and the place of Calvin's formative exile.
biblical_def: Strasbourg was a free imperial city on the Rhine that became one of the chief centres of the early Reformation under the leadership of Martin Bucer, and a place of decisive importance in the formation of John Calvin. When Calvin was expelled from Geneva in 1538, he spent three formative years (1538-1541) at Strasbourg, pastoring the congregation of French refugees, where he matured as a pastor, married, refined his liturgy and his thought, and learned much from Bucer's wisdom before returning to Geneva. The dictionary honours Strasbourg for two enduring contributions. First, it was a haven and school for the Reformed cause, a city of refuge where the gospel was preached and refugees for conscience' sake found welcome—God being a refuge and strength to His people. Second, it was a cradle of Reformed worship and especially of metrical psalm-singing: at Strasbourg Calvin developed the practice of congregational singing of the Psalms in the people's own tongue, a practice he carried to Geneva and that spread through the Reformed churches, embodying the conviction that the true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth, all the earth singing unto the LORD a new song. The dictionary marks Strasbourg as a witness to the breadth of the Reformation beyond its famous centres, and to the providence of God in Calvin's exile: what seemed a defeat—his expulsion from Geneva—God used to season and prepare him through the Strasbourg years for his greater later labours. Strasbourg stands for the Reformed recovery of intelligible, congregational, psalm-singing worship and for the hospitality of a city that sheltered the persecuted people of God.
webster_summary: The Rhine city, a chief early-Reformation centre under Bucer and the place of Calvin's formative 1538-1541 exile; a haven for refugees and a cradle of Reformed worship and congregational metrical psalm-singing.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Reformed reform of worship. At Strasbourg, Calvin developed the practice of congregational metrical psalm-singing in the people's own tongue, against both the Latin chant of Rome that the people could not understand and the silent spectatorship of the medieval Mass. Here the conviction took form that the true worshippers worship in spirit and in truth, that all the earth is to sing unto the LORD, and that the song of the church belongs to the whole congregation. The practice spread from Strasbourg through Geneva to the Reformed churches and shaped Protestant worship for centuries.

Strasbourg also displays the providence of God in the lives of His servants. Calvin's expulsion from Geneva in 1538 seemed a defeat; yet God used the three Strasbourg years to season him—pastoring refugees, marrying, learning from Bucer, maturing in thought and practice—and prepared him thereby for his far greater later labours. What looked like a closed door was God's schooling. The dictionary marks Strasbourg as a city of refuge that sheltered the persecuted people of God and as the cradle of intelligible, congregational, psalm-singing worship, honouring both its hospitality and its recovery of the worship Scripture commands.

etymology: From the convent of Port-Royal near Paris, the spiritual centre of French Jansenism in the seventeenth century, associated with Blaise Pascal.
biblical_def: Port-Royal was a convent near Paris that became, in the seventeenth century, the spiritual and intellectual centre of French Jansenism, the Augustinian reform movement within the Roman Catholic Church associated with Blaise Pascal and the theologians of the “Port-Royal logic.” The Jansenists, drawing on Augustine's doctrines of sin and grace, recovered against the prevailing Jesuit theology much that the Reformed also hold: the depth of human depravity, the bondage of the will, the necessity and efficacy of sovereign grace, and predestination. The dictionary treats Port-Royal with a careful, sympathetic discrimination. There is much in the Jansenist movement the dictionary commends, for it stood for the very truths of grace that Rome had largely abandoned: that no man can come to Christ except the Father draw him, that salvation is not by works of righteousness but according to His mercy, and that He which begins a good work will perform it. These are the doctrines of grace, and the dictionary rejoices wherever they are found. Yet Port-Royal remained within the Roman communion, never breaking from the papacy, the Mass, or the sacramental system, and so its recovery of Augustinian grace was hindered and incomplete, condemned at last by Rome itself. The dictionary marks Port-Royal as a sobering and hopeful witness: hopeful, that the truth of sovereign grace cannot be wholly extinguished and broke out even within Rome; sobering, that to recover the doctrines of grace while remaining bound to a system that denies justification by faith alone is to build on a divided foundation. The Lord knoweth them that are His, and there were doubtless His own at Port-Royal; yet the dictionary holds that the doctrines of grace are rightly housed only in a church reformed by the whole Word of God.
webster_summary: The convent near Paris that was the centre of French Jansenism, the Augustinian movement (associated with Pascal) that recovered the doctrines of grace within Rome; commended for those truths, yet hindered by remaining bound to the Roman system.

corruption_summary: Port-Royal recovered the doctrines of grace yet remained bound to the Roman system—the papacy, the Mass, the sacramental scheme—so that its Augustinian revival was hindered, incomplete, and condemned by Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary commends much in Port-Royal and the Jansenist movement it housed. Against the man-exalting theology of the Jesuits, the Jansenists recovered from Augustine the very truths the Reformed confess: the depth of human depravity, the bondage of the will, the sovereignty and efficacy of grace, and predestination. That no man comes to Christ but as the Father draws him, that God saves not by works but according to His mercy, that He who begins the good work will finish it—these are the doctrines of grace, and the dictionary rejoices that they broke out even within Rome, a proof that the truth of sovereign grace cannot be wholly extinguished.

Yet the dictionary marks the limitation that made the Jansenist recovery hindered and finally tragic. Port-Royal never broke from the Roman communion: it kept the papacy, the Mass, the sacramental system, and the Tridentine framework that denies justification by faith alone. To recover the doctrines of grace while remaining bound to a church that anathematized the gospel of grace is to build on a divided foundation, and Rome itself eventually condemned and dispersed them. The Lord knoweth them that are His, and there were surely His own at Port-Royal; but the dictionary holds that the doctrines of grace are rightly and safely housed only in a church reformed by the whole counsel of God, not in one that confesses sovereign grace with one breath and denies justification by faith with the next.

pos: proper noun (a French mathematician and apologist)
etymology: Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), the French mathematician, physicist, and Christian apologist of the Jansenist circle, author of the Pensées and the Provincial Letters.
biblical_def: Blaise Pascal (1623-1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, and Christian thinker of extraordinary genius, associated with the Jansenist circle of Port-Royal, whose religious writings—chiefly the Pensées (Thoughts) and the Provincial Letters—remain among the most penetrating in Christian literature. After a profound conversion experience in 1654, recorded on a parchment he sewed into his coat (the “Memorial”: “Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars”), Pascal devoted his powers to the defence of the faith. The dictionary honours much in Pascal. He grasped, against the rationalism of his age, that the things of God are not reached by unaided reason but are spiritually discerned, for the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit; that God hides Himself from the wise and prudent and reveals Himself to babes; that the heart is deceitful above all and that man is at once wretched and great, a fallen creature made for God. His famous “wager” and his maxim that “the heart has its reasons which reason knows not” press the limits of mere intellect and the necessity of a God-given faith. The dictionary marks the cautions a Reformed reader must keep. Pascal was a Roman Catholic and a Jansenist, and his apologetic, for all its brilliance, is not free of his communion's errors; the wager, taken alone, can be mistaken for a prudential gamble rather than the venture of true faith. Yet read with discernment, Pascal is a profound witness to human depravity and divine grace, to the insufficiency of reason and the necessity of revelation—a brilliant mind brought low before the God of Abraham, not the god of the philosophers.
webster_summary: Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), French mathematician and Christian apologist of the Jansenist circle, author of the Pensées; honoured for his witness to human depravity, the limits of reason, and the necessity of grace, read with caution as a Roman Catholic Jansenist.

corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary honours much in Pascal. Against the proud rationalism of his age, he saw that the things of God are not scaled by unaided reason but spiritually discerned, that God hides Himself from the wise and prudent and reveals Himself to babes, that the human heart is deceitful above all and man at once wretched and great—a ruined creature made for God. His witness to human depravity, to the insufficiency of reason, and to the necessity of a faith God must give places him near the Reformed estimate of fallen man, and his religious genius has profited the church far beyond his own communion.

Yet the dictionary keeps the cautions a Reformed reader must. Pascal was a Roman Catholic and a Jansenist, and his thought, for all its brilliance, is not free of his communion's errors and ambiguities. His celebrated “wager,” isolated from the rest of his thought, can be misread as a cold prudential gamble—bet on God because the odds favour it—rather than the venture of a faith that God Himself works in the heart; true faith is not a calculation of self-interest but the gift of God. Read with discernment, however, Pascal remains a profound witness to the doctrines of grace, a towering intellect brought low before the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, not the god of the philosophers and scholars.

etymology: From Bosnia; the independent medieval church of Bosnia, of disputed character, sometimes linked to the dualist Bogomil heresy, flourishing roughly from the twelfth to the fifteenth century.
biblical_def: The Bosnian Church was an independent medieval church body in the kingdom of Bosnia, flourishing roughly from the twelfth to the fifteenth century, standing apart from both Rome and Constantinople, and of much-disputed character. Some historians have linked it to the dualist Bogomil heresy—a movement akin to the Cathars, teaching two eternal principles of good and evil, an evil material creation, and a docetic Christ—while others judge it to have been a schismatic but broadly orthodox monastic church with peculiar customs. The historical evidence is fragmentary, and the dictionary treats the question with due caution, neither asserting more than the sources warrant nor passing over the doctrinal issue at stake. What the dictionary will name plainly is the error of dualism, if the Bogomil link be granted. Dualism, in any form, is a corruption of the biblical doctrine of creation: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth; by Christ were all things created, visible and invisible; every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused; and God saw everything that He had made, and it was very good. There are not two eternal principles, but one God who made all things, and a creation good in its origin though fallen by sin. To make matter evil in itself is to deny the goodness of the Creator and the reality of the incarnation, in which the Son took true flesh. The dictionary marks the Bosnian Church as a sober case-study: a church cut off from the wider body and from the full light of Scripture drifted into obscurity and, perhaps, into heresy, and under Ottoman conquest its people largely passed into Islam. The lesson it teaches is the danger of a Christianity severed from the Word and the catholic faith, and the abiding truth that the one God made all things good.

corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary treats the disputed character of the Bosnian Church with due caution, for the historical evidence is fragmentary and scholars differ on whether it was a dualist Bogomil body or a schismatic but broadly orthodox monastic church with peculiar customs. The dictionary will not assert more than the sources warrant. But the doctrinal issue, if the Bogomil link be granted, is grave and worth naming. Dualism teaches two eternal principles of good and evil, an evil material world made by a lesser or evil power, and a Christ who only seemed to take flesh. This is a fundamental corruption of the faith.

Against all dualism the dictionary sets the plain word of Scripture: in the beginning the one God created the heaven and the earth; by Christ were all things created, visible and invisible; every creature of God is good; and God saw everything He had made, and it was very good. There are not two eternal principles but one Creator, and the creation is good in its origin, marred only by the sin that entered it. To call matter evil is to slander the Creator and to deny the incarnation, in which the Son took real human flesh. The Bosnian Church, whatever its precise doctrine, stands as a sober case-study of a Christianity cut off from the wider body and the full light of Scripture, drifting into obscurity and, under Ottoman conquest, largely into Islam—a warning of the danger of a church severed from the Word and the catholic faith.

etymology: The Scots Confession of 1560, drafted by John Knox and five others (the “Six Johns”) and adopted by the Scottish Parliament as the first confession of the Reformed Church of Scotland.
biblical_def: The Scots Confession is the first confession of faith of the Reformed Church of Scotland, drawn up in 1560 by John Knox and five companions (the “Six Johns”) and ratified by the Scottish Parliament in the same year, when Scotland officially embraced the Reformation. Written swiftly, in vigorous and warm-hearted language, it set forth in twenty-five articles the Reformed faith—the Trinity, creation, the fall, the covenant, election, the incarnation and work of Christ, justification by faith, the church, the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, and the civil magistrate. The dictionary honours the Scots Confession as a stirring early monument of the Reformed faith in Britain, marked by its readiness always to give an answer for the hope that is in the church—indeed its preface invites correction from the Word of God, declaring that if any man note in the confession any article contrary to God's Word, they would amend it. It confessed with the heart unto righteousness and with the mouth made confession unto salvation, building the church upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ being the chief corner stone, against the rock of which the gates of hell shall not prevail. The dictionary notes that the Scots Confession was later largely superseded in Scotland by the Westminster Confession (1647), which became the principal subordinate standard of Scottish Presbyterianism; yet the Scots Confession remains honoured as the heroic first fruit of the Scottish Reformation. The dictionary, holding the 1689 Baptist Confession as its own primary standard, receives the Scots Confession as a faithful Reformed witness, differing on baptism and the magistrate, but one in the great gospel of free and sovereign grace.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the value and proper use of confessions of faith. The modern anti-creedal spirit, raising the cry “no creed but the Bible,” despises documents like the Scots Confession as mere human inventions that bind the conscience and rival Scripture. The Scots Confession itself answers this charge in its own humble preface, inviting any man to note from the Word of God any article amiss, that it might be amended. A true confession does not rival Scripture but summarizes and confesses it, a subordinate standard always under the Word, by which the church is ready to give an answer for the hope that is in her.

The dictionary honours the Scots Confession as the heroic first-fruit of the Scottish Reformation, written swiftly and warmly by Knox and his companions when a nation turned from Rome to the gospel. It receives it as a faithful Reformed witness, building the church on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ the chief corner stone. Holding the 1689 Baptist Confession as its own primary subordinate standard, the dictionary differs from the Scots Confession on baptism and the civil magistrate, yet rejoices in its agreement on the great gospel of free and sovereign grace, and commends the recovery of confessional Christianity against the rootless anti-creedalism of the age.

etymology: The sixteenth-century Reformation in Scotland, led chiefly by John Knox, by which the nation broke from Rome and established the Reformed (Presbyterian) Church of Scotland in 1560.
biblical_def: The Scottish Reformation was the sixteenth-century movement by which Scotland broke from the Roman Catholic Church and established the Reformed faith, reaching its decisive triumph in 1560 when the Scottish Parliament abolished the Mass and papal jurisdiction and adopted the Scots Confession. Its great leader was John Knox, the fiery preacher who, after years of exile (including labour in Geneva under Calvin, whose church he called “the most perfect school of Christ” since the apostles), returned to Scotland and preached the Reformation into being with a boldness that feared no king nor queen. The dictionary honours the Scottish Reformation as a mighty work of God, in which the truth made a nation free: where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty, and the knowledge of the truth set Scotland free from the bondage of Rome. Knox and the Reformers spoke of God's testimonies before kings and were not ashamed, standing fast in the liberty wherewith Christ makes free. The Reformation gave Scotland a Reformed and Presbyterian church, a confession, a book of discipline, and a vision of national education and godliness that shaped the nation for centuries. The dictionary marks the Scottish Reformation against the secular history that reduces it to mere politics or social upheaval, and against the romanticizing that forgets its real cost in blood and conflict. It was, at its heart, a recovery of the gospel: justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, the rule of Christ over His church, and the worship of God according to His Word. The dictionary, in the Reformed and Baptist line that flowed from it, honours the Scottish Reformation as a great deliverance, while holding that the reform of the church is never finished but must go on by the Word until the church is wholly conformed to Christ.
webster_summary: The 16th-century movement, led by John Knox, by which Scotland broke from Rome and established the Reformed faith in 1560; a mighty work of God in which the truth made a nation free, recovering the gospel and the authority of Scripture.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Scottish Reformation was, at its heart, a recovery of the gospel. Secular history reduces it to political maneuvering, social upheaval, or the ambitions of nobles, treating its theology as a pretext for power. The dictionary affirms the political and social dimensions while denying the reduction: the Reformation was driven by the recovered truths of justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, the rule of Christ over His church, and the worship of God according to His Word. Knox preached doctrine, not merely policy, and the nation was changed by the knowledge of the truth that makes men free.

The opposite error romanticizes the Reformation into a tidy heroic legend, forgetting its real cost in conflict, exile, and blood, and the imperfections of its leaders and settlements. The dictionary honours the Scottish Reformation as a mighty deliverance of God—where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty—while remembering that it was hard-won and that the reform of the church is never complete. Knox and his fellows spoke God's testimonies before kings and were not ashamed, and gave Scotland a Reformed church, a confession, and a vision of godliness. The dictionary, in the line that flowed from them, honours the work while holding that the church must go on being reformed by the Word until she is wholly conformed to Christ.

etymology: From the Greek presbyteros (elder); the system of church government by elders and graded assemblies (sessions, presbyteries, synods, general assemblies), held by the Presbyterian and Reformed churches.
biblical_def: Presbyterianism is the system of church government in which the church is ruled by elders (Greek presbyteroi) gathered in graded assemblies—the local session, the regional presbytery, the broader synod, and the general assembly—held by the Presbyterian and many Reformed churches as the New Testament pattern. It rests on several biblical convictions: that the church is governed not by a single bishop nor by the congregation alone but by a plurality of elders; that elders were ordained in every church (Acts 14:23) and in every city (Titus 1:5); that the office is conferred with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery; and that disputed matters are settled by assemblies of apostles and elders gathered together, as at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15). The dictionary treats Presbyterianism with respect as a serious and biblically-argued polity within the Reformed family, the government of the Westminster churches and the Church of Scotland. Yet the dictionary, holding the 1689 Baptist Confession and the congregational polity of the Baptists, differs from Presbyterianism on the question of church government and on the related matter of the subjects of baptism. Where Presbyterianism gathers local churches under the binding authority of higher courts, the Baptist tradition holds to the independence of the local congregation under Christ, governed by its own elders and members, associating with other churches voluntarily rather than under a binding hierarchy of assemblies. The dictionary marks this as a difference among brethren who hold the same gospel of sovereign grace and the same Reformed doctrine: Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists are agreed on the great matters of salvation and divided on the polity and the subjects of baptism, contending as friends over the New Testament pattern of the church.
webster_summary: Church government by elders in graded assemblies (session, presbytery, synod, general assembly), held by Presbyterian and Reformed churches as the New Testament pattern (Acts 14:23; 15:6); respected by the dictionary, which holds the Baptist congregational polity.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the dictionary, holding Baptist congregational polity, differs from Presbyterianism on church government and the subjects of baptism, as a difference among brethren in the same gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter at issue is not a corruption to be rebutted but a difference among brethren who hold the same gospel. The dictionary respects Presbyterianism as a serious, biblically-argued polity within the Reformed family, the government of the Westminster churches and the Kirk of Scotland, resting on real New Testament evidence for rule by a plurality of elders, the laying on of hands by the presbytery, and the settling of disputes by assemblies of elders. It is no light or unscriptural scheme, and the dictionary contends with it as with friends, not foes.

Yet the dictionary, holding the 1689 Baptist Confession and the congregational polity of the Baptists, differs on the question of church government and the related question of baptism. Where Presbyterianism binds local churches under the authority of higher courts—presbyteries and assemblies—the Baptist tradition holds to the independence of the local congregation under Christ its only Head, governed by its own elders and members, and associating with sister churches voluntarily rather than under a binding hierarchy. And where Presbyterianism baptizes the infant children of believers, the Baptist baptizes believers only. The dictionary marks these as differences among those agreed on the great gospel of sovereign grace and the doctrines of the Reformed faith—Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists contending as brethren over the New Testament pattern of the church, not over the way of salvation.
